trials.boundary: RUN, where the lead says in its own last sentence that it was not. Over the alternating dz/doubling walk: seed 0 gives period 2; seed 2 first returns at index 6, which is EVEN and therefore out of phase; seeds 1 and 3 never return within 24. period() accepts a return only at an ODD index — a completed dz-then-doubling pair — so 0 for seeds 1, 2 and 3 is an accurate report that no in-phase period exists. The lead's correction of its own earlier false claim is confirmed figure for figure. AND THE COSMETIC HALF DOES NOT SURVIVE MEASUREMENT EITHER: period() returns i+1 with i >= 0, so its least possible value is 1 and 0 can never be a real period. The sentinel is unambiguous, which is exactly what the two-state instruments found this week were not. trials.lead: gpuPresence DETECTS an accelerator and nothing in the tree dispatches to one. The field is honest but the gap is permanent until something uses it
trials.boundary: MEASURED, on real hardware, through the browser harness at /os — the first time anything in this repository has run on a GPU. The shader AGREED with the CPU reference element for element at every size, so the dispatch is correct. And the CPU won at every size: 1525.88x at 1,024 elements, 10.39x at 16,384, 4.84x at 262,144 and 2.72x at 1,048,576. The prediction recorded before the measurement was that the CPU would win below roughly a hundred thousand elements; it in fact wins at a million, the margin narrowing but never crossing. A dispatch is a buffer write, a submit and a readback, and that fixed cost never amortises against 37-83 ns/element on work this shape. The dispatch stays as a MEASURED negative result rather than a capability: it is real, it is correct, and it is slower. — CORRECTED THE SAME DAY, and the refutation above measured the wrong arrangement. Those figures are the GPU used ALONE, awaited immediately, which idles the CPU and can only lose. Split across both processors with the dispatch submitted first and the CPU share computed while it is in flight, the involution BEATS the CPU alone at 1,048,576 elements: 170.70 ms for CPU alone against 134.90 ms at a 10% GPU share (1.27x), 141.10 ms at 50% (1.21x) and 159.40 ms at 25% (1.07x), with correctness holding at every split. It loses again at 75% and 100%. The ordering is NON-MONOTONIC, so run-to-run noise is comparable to the effect and no optimal split is claimed — only that the involution can beat either processor alone, which is the opposite of what the first measurement concluded.

trials.lead: deploy-run reports COMPLETE and exits 0 while four steps inside it FAILED: always_use_https could not authenticate for uuidna.com, uuidna.net, uuidna.org and perma.family. The redirect is in fact enforced (http answers 301), so the zone setting was already on and only the verification failed — but the run could not tell the difference and said nothing
trials.boundary: THE DILEMMA IT POSED WAS FALSE, and both horns were bad. It owed "a token with zone scope, OR a non-zero exit when a hardening step fails". The second horn is the one that looks principled and it is a trap: the writes fail for want of scope on every workstation run, the redirect is enforced regardless, so exiting non-zero converts a false all-clear into a false alarm that blocks correct ships — and a step that cries wolf on every run is a step people route around. Fixed 2026-09-01 by a third route the lead did not consider: when the API write is refused, ASK THE ZONE WHAT IT DOES. An http request answering 301 to an https location proves the redirect is in force, which is a stronger claim than the write's own success (that proves only acceptance, not application). All four apexes — uuidna.com, uuidna.net, uuidna.org, perma.family — now report ENFORCED verified by effect, and an apex serving plain http joins the hard-fail set beside the 522 class.

trials.lead: THE RATCHET IS VALIDATED AND ITS FIRST STEP IS TOO SLOW FOR A TAB. Measured in a real browser 2026-09-01 (PortsConsole on /os): chatSend #0, which derives the session with PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations in pure TypeScript, cost 25.7 s; chatSend #1 on the same session, rotating the key by its step, cost 2.4 ms. About 10,700x. The design is exactly right — the two coins are paid ONCE and every later message is free — and that is the captain's law in one measurement: highest speed comes at highest security, by design.
trials.boundary: Wall removed 2026-09-01 without touching the iteration count. crypt.ts already cached the derived key and already reached node:crypto on Node; a browser has crypto.subtle.deriveBits, which is async and so could not slot into a synchronous send — but it does not need to, because an async WARMER can derive with the host primitive and fill that cache before any send. Measured: chatSend #0 went 25.7 s (background tab) to 1.1 ms. The host derivation is verified BYTE-FOR-BYTE against the pure implementation at the full 600,000 iterations, and a host that ever disagrees is refused for the whole process — slow and correct beats fast and unopenable. The two coins are still paid; they are paid by hardware that has the instruction.
